What happens when you call us?

A volunteer answers

A trained volunteer answers with something like “Samaritans, can I help you?” You don’t need to prepare anything before you call or know exactly what to say.

You talk, we listen

We listen to what’s happening in your life and how you’re feeling. We may ask questions to help you explore your thoughts and talk through your experiences.

We give you space

There’s no pressure to explain everything at once or find the right words. You can pause, take the time you need and end the call at any time.

We don’t judge you

You can talk openly about your thoughts and feelings, including thoughts of suicide. We listen without judgement and don’t tell you what you should do.

What can I speak to Samaritans about?

People contact us with all sorts of concerns. You could be going through something new or have been struggling to cope for some time. Either way, we’re here if you feel you need some extra support.

Common reasons people contact us include:

  • relationship and family problems
  • loss, including the death of a friend or family member
  • financial worries
  • job-related stress
  • college or study-related stress
  • loneliness and isolation
  • depression and other mental health problems
  • physical illness, pain or disability
  • addiction, including problems with alcohol, drugs or gambling
  • thoughts of suicide

If what’s getting to you isn’t on this list, please still get in touch.

We listen without judgement and help you explore your thoughts and feelings. We won’t make decisions for you or tell you what to do.

If you’re looking for advice or specialist help, we may be able to give you contact details for organisations that can help with your situation.

Stories of hope

Explore stories from people who contacted Samaritans and discover how it helped.

Efe’s story "Connecting with people is probably the best thing in the world. Just talking to another human being who wants to help you can really carry you such a long way." Sarah’s story "Sometimes, when you say something out loud it takes power away from it." Elsa's story "There are lots of different pressures I face being online, particularly on social media. This can be anything from comparing my life to my friends or influencers, to comparing my appearance and the way I look."
